title: Serverless & FaaS Fundamentals
summary: What 'serverless' actually means and the event-driven, pay-per-invocation execution model underneath every FaaS platform.

slides.markdown:
**Serverless** doesn't mean no servers — it means you never provision, patch, or scale them yourself. The provider runs your code on infrastructure it manages entirely; you write functions, upload them, and let events invoke them.

- You still pay for compute — just per **invocation**, not per **server-hour**.
- The abstraction ladder: IaaS gives you the server, PaaS gives you the runtime, serverless/FaaS gives you just the **function boundary**.
- Ops work doesn't disappear — it shifts to a different set of concerns (cold starts, concurrency, vendor APIs).

**FaaS** (Functions as a Service) makes the function — not the VM, not the container — the unit you deploy and the unit you're billed for. You write a handler (`handleRequest(event)`), the platform packages it, and each invocation runs in an isolated execution environment the platform manages.

This is a real shift from PaaS: a PaaS app is one long-running process serving many requests; a FaaS function is invoked fresh (or reused, opportunistically) per event, with the platform deciding how many run in parallel.

A FaaS function has no listening process waiting for requests — it **runs in response to a trigger**: an HTTP call, a message landing in a queue, a file uploaded to storage, a scheduled timer. Nothing runs, and nothing costs money, until an event fires.

This is the opposite of a traditional server, always running whether or not it's doing useful work. It also means the platform, not your code, decides concurrency: ten simultaneous uploads can spin up ten parallel invocations without you provisioning anything.

An always-on VM bills by the hour whether it's serving 1,000 requests or zero. FaaS bills by **invocation and execution time** — you pay only for the milliseconds your code actually ran, typically metered in small increments.

This is why serverless is cheap for spiky, low-average-utilization workloads (an API that bursts once an hour) and can become expensive at constant high volume — at that point you're paying a per-request premium for capacity you'd use every second anyway.

A function instance can be frozen, reused for a later invocation, or destroyed entirely between calls — there's no guarantee any two invocations share the same process. Anything stored in local memory or on local disk **may or may not survive** to the next call, and code must never depend on it doing so.

Any state that needs to persist — a counter, a session, a cache — has to live somewhere external: a database, a managed cache, or object storage. Treating local memory as durable is the single most common serverless bug.

slides.subTitle: An image-resize function
slides.markdown:
A photo-sharing app needs a thumbnail generated every time a user uploads an image. Instead of running a server that polls for new uploads, a function is configured to trigger **on file upload** to a storage bucket.

The event carries the file's location; the function reads it, resizes it, writes the thumbnail back to storage, and exits. It runs for maybe 200ms, a thousand times a day or a million — the code and the bill scale identically without a single server ever being provisioned or watched.

slides.subTitle: "No infrastructure to think about"
slides.markdown:
The wrong belief: going serverless means there's no infrastructure to think about. In reality, you've traded server management for a different set of operational concerns — cold-start latency, per-invocation concurrency limits, execution time caps, vendor-specific event formats, and a stateless model that breaks code written for a long-running process.

The correct model: serverless removes *provisioning and patching*, not *operations*. Monitoring, debugging, and capacity thinking are all still required — they just look different.
